source: Schwid and O'Donnell (1992) Anesthesiologists' management of simulated critical incidents (Anesthesiology 76:495-501)
finding: In a computer anaesthesia simulator, fixation errors (failure to revise a plan when cues were inconsistent) were made by 63% of subjects. Experience did not protect. Subjects who gathered more information in the anaphylaxis case diagnosed it more often.
numbers: N=30 (10 residents, 10 faculty, 10 private practice). Fixation 63% of subjects. Anaphylaxis correctly diagnosed 40%; MI adequately treated 27%; cardiac arrest per ACLS 30%.
quote: Fixation errors or failure to revise a plan in the presence of inconsistent cues were made by 63% of subjects.
limits: Abstract opened (PubMed text, truncated at 250 words); the full paper was not. 63% is a share of subjects who made at least one fixation error across several scenarios, not a per-case rate. Small N, 1992 PC simulator, no control for scenario difficulty.
agent_relevance: Closes the 'is 63% real' part of gap 10: yes, and it is per subject. Do not compare it with Gaba's 20%, which is per incident. Useful only as a human baseline that fixation is common; the info-gathering link supports an O-probe step.

source: DeAnda and Gaba (1990) Unplanned incidents during comprehensive anesthesia simulation (Anesth Analg 71:77-82)
finding: Fixation errors were about one fifth of all unplanned incidents in residents' simulated cases; human errors were two thirds; equipment failure was rare.
numbers: 19 simulations, 132 unplanned incidents (73% simple, 27% critical). Causes: human error 65.9% (87), fixation 20.5% (27, mean 1.42 per simulation), unknown 10.6%, equipment 3% (4). First- and second-year residents.
quote: document fixation errors as a frequent cause of incidents in anesthesia
limits: Abstract opened. Denominator is incidents, not people or cases. Residents only. Modified critical-incident coding by the authors.
agent_relevance: Settles gap 10 for Gaba: the ~20% is a share of incidents (20.5% of 132), so it is not comparable with Schwid's 63% of subjects. Rates depend on the denominator; our agent test should report both per-run and per-incident rates.

source: Cheng, Zhu, Zhao, Arora (2026) Contextual Drag: How Errors in the Context Affect LLM Reasoning (arXiv 2602.04288)
finding: A wrong earlier attempt left in the context pulls later answers toward the same kind of error, even when the draft is labelled wrong and even when the model itself says it is wrong. Two mitigations help but do not restore the clean-slate score: rewriting/filtering the draft, and a trained 'reset to clean slate' behaviour.
numbers: 11 models, 8 tasks, 16 samples per question. Typical drop 10-20%; GPT-OSS-20B HMMT25 58.63 clean -> 20.54 with one wrong draft (1F). Explicit verification of the draft in the prompt (1F-V): 42.26. REVISE 62.20, FILTER 45.83 (FILTER recovers about 66% of the loss; REVISE overshoots here). GPQA GPT-OSS-20B: clean 46.97, 1F 16.86, 1F-V 26.66, REVISE 33.33, FILTER 43.70. Nemotron-32B HMMT25 FILTER 91.96 vs clean 80.36. Qwen3-8B CruxEval clean 67.49, 1F 40.09, REVISE 49.00, FILTER 51.80. Targeted SFT on GPT-OSS-20B: AIME24 under 1F 17.5 -> 40.6.
quote: a draft that is accurately rejected could still shape the model's reasoning trajectory
limits: Wrong drafts are the model's own earlier failures on math/science/code, not a 'dropped hypothesis' in a diagnosis. Open-weight reasoning models mostly; proprietary models only on competition math, and their drop is small (GPT-5 AIME24 88.75 -> 88.13). Denoising uses several extra passes; no token counts reported. The self-detected-error analysis assumes an oracle filter.
agent_relevance: Strongest direct LLM evidence for gaps 1 and 4. Saying 'this claim is wrong' (or even finding the replacement) is not enough; the dropped claim keeps steering. What worked best was removing the draft text and re-deriving from a strategy (FILTER) or a clean restart. For our agent: when a hypothesis is dropped, delete its text from the working context rather than only annotate it. Costs more passes; test at equal tokens.

source: Jung and Son (2026) How Much Heavy Lifting Can an Agent Harness Do? Measuring the LLM's Residual Role in a Planning Agent (arXiv 2604.07236)
finding: One of the few papers that states a numeric reframing trigger for an LLM agent: revise only after a sustained low-confidence streak, with a cooldown. The trigger was not tuned; it misfires on transient dips, and the LLM-backed revision helped F1 slightly but lowered win rate.
numbers: Noisy Collaborative Battleship, 54 games (18 boards x 3 seeds). Defaults: EMA 0.25, streak threshold 2 turns, cooldown 3 turns, min revision delta 0.01, confidence threshold 0.72. Adding planning to a belief-only harness: win rate 50.0% -> 74.1% with zero LLM calls. LLM revision gate (threshold 1.0) fires on 4.3% of turns, F1 0.557 (highest of the reflective family), win rate 53.7% (lowest); at 18 games the win-rate ordering reversed. Three boards were over-revised on a transient dip.
limits: Trigger is on model confidence from prediction error, not on a count of unexplained cues. Board game, a 4B local LLM (gemma4:e4b), thresholds are defaults not optima, win-rate effect unstable between 18 and 54 games.
agent_relevance: Answers gap 2 only in part: a streak rule (2 consecutive misses) plus cooldown is a workable, cheap, LLM-free trigger shape, and over-triggering on transient dips is a real cost. No evidence yet for a specific count of unexplained cues in diagnosis. Treat 'streak>=2, cooldown 3' as a starting value to test, not a finding.

source: Bertolazzi, Tentori, Bernardi (2026) FalsifyBench: Evaluating Inductive Reasoning in LLMs with Rule Discovery Games (arXiv 2606.04751)
finding: In a Wason 2-4-6 style game over WordNet categories, models that test outside their current hypothesis (negative tests) win more. The link is correlational: no run forced a disconfirming test.
numbers: 12 LLMs, 1,200 games. Success: GPT-5.2-Chat 75%, GPT-OSS-120B 68%, best instruction-tuned DeepSeek-V3.1 41%, others 33-35%; GPT-5-Nano 12%, Qwen3.5-9B 21%. Confirmation bias (share of positive tests) vs success Spearman rho -0.779 (p=0.003); vs conclusive falsification rate rho -0.937 (p<0.001). Bayesian logistic model: confirmation bias coefficient -4.15 (OR 0.016); oracle error no credible effect. Conclusive falsification: GPT-OSS-20B 59.2%, GPT-OSS-120B 53.4%, GPT-5.2-Chat 49.5%, Llama-4-Maverick 18.0%.
quote: models that actively seek to falsify their hypotheses consistently outperform those that primarily seek confirmation
limits: Observational across models (n=12 for the correlations). Rule-guessing game with a clean oracle; hypotheses are always nested in the target so negative tests are uniquely informative. Failure also came from poor hypothesis paths, not only from confirmation bias.
agent_relevance: Gap 8 stays open. The result is only 'models that test more negatively win'; nobody has forced the behaviour or moved it to diagnosis. A diagnosis analogue needs a task where the right next test is the one the leading hypothesis predicts will fail. Keep O-test as a hypothesis to test, not a proven operator.

source: Chinn (1993) The Role of Anomalous Data in Theory Change: A Cognitive Analysis (Third International Seminar on Misconceptions)
finding: Primary author's statement of the seven responses to anomalous data (ignore, reject, exclude, abeyance, reinterpret, peripheral theory change, theory change) and nine hypothesised factors that decide which one is used. Deep processing (having to justify the evaluation) raises theory change; independent replicated lines of evidence raise acceptance; unambiguous demonstrations beat ambiguous ones.
numbers: No response frequencies in this paper. Gives the taxonomy, nine factors, and pointers to Chinn and Brewer 1992, 1993a-c for the experiments. Example: Johsua and Dupin electricity students resisted until an analogy made the new theory intelligible.
quote: It is often more rational to discount a piece of data than to accept it and change theories.
limits: Theory/framework paper by Chinn alone; factors are 'hypothesized'. The 1998 empirical test (JRST 35:623-654) could not be opened (publisher returns 403), so the response frequencies in claim K02 are still unverified.
agent_relevance: Confirms the taxonomy is a seven-way list and that discounting data can be rational. For our agent: the factors that raise theory change (justify to others, independent replication, intelligible alternative) map to O-reframe preconditions. Gap 6 stays open for the numbers.

source: Meister, Krell, Gohner, Upmeier zu Belzen (2021) Pre-service Biology Teachers' Responses to First-Hand Anomalous Data During Modelling Processes (Res Sci Educ 51:1459-1479)
finding: When people met their own anomalous data in a black-box modelling task, they most often explained it as method error (imprecise measuring) and rarely changed their assumptions. When the anomaly clashed with a model they had built, they explained it with the model or changed/rejected the model more often.
numbers: N=11 pre-service teachers, video protocols. Anomaly vs expected data pattern: 46 situations recognised; 20 explained by method issues, 7 by the model, 2 led to changed assumptions. Anomaly vs own developed model: 14 recognised; 1 method explanation, 6 model explanation, 6 model modification, 4 model rejection; in half of the 14 no explanation was given. Anomaly vs general logic: 4.
limits: N=11 with qualitative content coding, one task. Counts are situations, not people. Coded with the Chinn and Brewer scheme but not the full 7-way list.
agent_relevance: Independent, small human replication of the 'explain it away as measurement error' pattern, and a boundary condition: conflict with one's own built model drives revision more than conflict with an expected pattern. Suggests an agent should record its explicit model of the situation so later anomalies hit a model, not just an expectation.

source: Hemmerich, Van Voorhis, Wiley (2016) Anomalous Evidence, Confidence Change, and Theory Change (Cognitive Science 40:1534-1560)
finding: Three experiments: confidence in a theory fell in proportion to the amount of anomalous evidence, and bigger confidence drops predicted theory change. Convergent evidence (different kinds) and an offered alternative theory gave larger confidence drops; convergent evidence also caused more theory change.
numbers: Abstract only: no sample sizes or effect sizes in the text opened. Exp 1 varied dose of anomalous evidence; Exp 2 convergent vs replicated; Exp 3 with vs without an alternative theory.
quote: larger decreases in confidence predicted theory changes
limits: Abstract opened (PubMed). Numbers not seen. Human lab task with an invented scenario.
agent_relevance: Best human evidence for gap 2: reframing follows a graded confidence loss that grows with the amount and the variety of anomalous cues, and an alternative theory speeds it. So a trigger could be a running 'confidence in current frame' score that unexplained cues of different kinds lower, not a bare count. No threshold value is given. Supports pairing O-reframe with a ready alternative.

source: Trickett, Trafton, Schunn, Harrison (2001) That's Odd! How Scientists Respond to Anomalous Data (CogSci 2001 proceedings)
finding: Scientists analysing their own data noticed anomalies and gave them much more follow-up than expected results, and proposed hypotheses for anomalies far more often. The hypotheses were built mostly from the visual display, not from domain theory.
numbers: 2 datasets (astronomy 27 noticings, physics 9), 3 scientists. Mean later references per noticed item: astronomy anomalies 7.6 vs expected 1.5; physics 3.0 vs 1.25 (t(28)=2.33, p<.05). Hypothesis proposed for anomalies much more often than for expected noticings (chi2(1)=7.5, p<.05). 4 of 5 anomaly hypotheses in astronomy drew on the display.
quote: the scientists noticed anomalies and paid more attention to them than to expected data
limits: Three experts, two domains, in-vivo protocols. Cites Dunbar (1997) for scientists dropping hypotheses quickly when results conflicted. Very small sample.
agent_relevance: Re-opened source behind K01 (notice, then local explain). Both noticing and local patching from the display are expert behaviour. The test for our agent is to score whether the explanation reaches the domain model or stays on the display.

source: Wang, Leong, Wang, Li (2026) Seeing Isn't Believing: Mitigating Belief Inertia via Active Intervention in Embodied Agents (arXiv 2604.17252)
finding: Embodied LLM agents often ignore an observation that contradicts their belief. A predict-then-compare step (Estimate, Verify, Update) beat generic multi-pass reflection at lower reasoning cost, and short context did not remove the inertia.
numbers: 100 neglect cases probed on ALFWorld: belief stays on the wrong side after the contradicting observation. With history cut to the last 2 turns, 95% of the cases still showed inertia. EVU gains: +6.8 points on seen, +9.21 on unseen splits; +10.37 training-based, +3.28 prompting-based. DeepSeek V3.2 on ALFWorld: Multiple Reflection 46.3 vs EVU 49.8 success with fewer reasoning tokens (read from an extracted table). Qwen2.5-3B: total tokens per task 1213.3 -> 892.9, turns 20.4 -> 18.2. ScienceWorld vs MEM1 summarisation: 67.1 -> 70.9 seen, 64.9 -> 70.8 unseen.
limits: Embodied text games, mostly small trained models; the generic-reflection control is one baseline. Author-run comparisons. Success deltas are small in the prompting case.
agent_relevance: Supports a surprise-triggered recheck for gaps 2 and 3: make the agent write the expected outcome before the action, then compare. The mismatch is a measurable trigger with a clean zero point, and it beat 'reflect again' at lower reasoning tokens. Good candidate for O-recheck.

source: Chen, Zhang, Ma, Li (2026) Hypothesis Graph Refinement: Hypothesis-Driven Exploration with Cascade Error Correction for Embodied Navigation (arXiv 2604.04108)
finding: When a prediction is refuted, retracting it together with everything built on it works better than deleting only the refuted node.
numbers: GOAT-Bench subset: full system SR 72.41 / SPL 56.22; w/o cascade correction SR 68.61; local delete only SR 70.85; w/o both 63.42. Cascade removes about 20% of redundant hypothesis nodes and cuts revisits to erroneous regions by 4.5x. Most cascades are shallow: depth 1 = 72%.
limits: Vision-language navigation with an explicit dependency graph; hypotheses are map labels, not diagnoses. Ablations are single runs from the authors.
agent_relevance: Mechanism for gap 1: dropping a hypothesis should also drop its dependents. Contextual drag (d03) shows annotation is not enough; this shows the structural fix. For the agent, keep a dependency list of conclusions built on each hypothesis and invalidate them together.

source: Fang et al. (2026) Benchmarking Multi-turn Medical Diagnosis: Hold, Lure, and Self-Correction (MINT, arXiv 2604.04325)
finding: Models answer diagnosis questions too early even when told to wait; strong lures such as lab results trigger it. Changing when the question appears fixes much of the loss. Models revise wrong answers upward more than right ones downward, but only after committing.
numbers: 1,035 cases, 11 LLMs. Over 55% of answers committed within the first two turns. Incorrect-to-correct revisions up to 10.6 times the rate of correct-to-incorrect. Average accuracy drop from early answering 24.2%. Asking the question last improves accuracy at first commitment by up to 62.6%; holding lab evidence for later prevents a drop of up to 23.3%. Guess rate before any evidence: Med42-70B 99.9%, GPT-5-mini 5.9%, Claude Sonnet 4.6 3.7%.
quote: models rush to answer before sufficient evidence has been observed
limits: Multiple-choice, evidence shards pre-cut, not an open tool environment. 'Wait' is an instruction in the prompt, not a forced step. Question-last changes the task, so it is a design fix, not a reasoning fix.
agent_relevance: Gaps 4 and 5. Two usable points: (1) an instruction to wait is weak, so withholding the commit question or the answer slot is stronger; (2) early commitment forecloses a latent ability to revise. For the agent: do not state a leading diagnosis until a minimum evidence set is in; keep an 'open' state.

source: Liu et al. (2026) AgentAbstain: Do LLM Agents Know When Not to Act? (arXiv 2607.10059)
finding: Paired tasks (should-act, near-identical should-abstain) in tool sandboxes show agents act when they should abstain. Abstention skill is mostly independent of task-solving skill. A common failure is post-hoc abstention: the irreversible action is taken first.
numbers: 263 paired tasks, 42 sandbox environments, 17 frontier LLMs, 4 harnesses. Best agent (Gemini 3.1 Pro) paired accuracy 59.5%. One scenario (S3): act side 90%, abstain side 41%. Annotators rate 94-98% of sampled tasks well designed.
limits: Synthetic sandboxes; paired accuracy rewards both sides, so a single abstain prompt cannot be judged from one number. No prompt-based abstain operator tested in the parts read.
agent_relevance: Gap 5, the agent-tool version we asked for: abstain is not fixed by capability, and over-acting is the default. The paired design (same task with and without the trigger) is the right evaluation for any abstain/clarify operator, since it scores the cost on answerable items together with the gain.

source: Luo, Wen, Wang (2026) Agentic Abstention: Do Agents Know When to Stop Instead of Act? (arXiv 2606.28733)
finding: Agents fail to stop when the task becomes infeasible only after interaction; some never abstain, others abstain only after many wasted steps. Bigger or more capable models sometimes abstain later. A stopping rule distilled from past trajectories (CONVOLVE) raises timely abstention without training.
numbers: 13 LLM-as-agent systems, 2 scaffolds, over 28,000 tasks (WebShop, terminal, QA from AbstentionBench). CONVOLVE on WebShop: Llama-3.3-70B timely recall 26.7 -> 57.4. Tuned on 500 abstain-only examples, 101 held out.
limits: CONVOLVE was tested on an abstain-only subset, so its cost on answerable tasks was not measured in what was read. Context-engineered rules are learned from the same task family.
agent_relevance: Gap 5: a learned stopping rule in context is the first agent-level abstain operator with a large measured gain, but its false-abstention cost is unknown. Run it on mixed answerable/unanswerable sets before adopting.

source: Yang et al. (2026) Agents' Overreliance on Unreliable Tools (arXiv 2609.05587)
finding: Agents adopt corrupted tool returns at high rates, and corrupted returns override answers the agents had right without tools. In reasoning traces the agent often doubts the return, sometimes states the correct value, and still passes the corrupted content on without warning: an explaining-away pattern. Prompts that tell the agent to verify cut adoption modestly with little loss on correct returns; comparing to prior knowledge cut more but also hurt correct returns.
numbers: 14 models, 3 tools. Mean adoption of corrupted return: search 68.0%, sub-agent 40.1%, code executor 35.5%. Warnings to the user in 4.2% of adopting final answers (1.5% without one outlier model). Prompt policies, mean over 6 models (P0 accuracy with correct return / P1 adoption with corrupted return): Search PLAIN 94.2/75.4, COMPARE 90.9/67.6, VERIFY 94.2/70.0, DISCLOSE 93.3/72.0. Sub-agent PLAIN 68.1/39.0, COMPARE 63.7/29.3, VERIFY 69.9/35.2. Code PLAIN 99.8/40.2, COMPARE 100.0/31.2, VERIFY 99.9/30.4. Reliability label 'Low' lowered adoption for all six models vs plain. SFT/DPO/GRPO gave limited gains.
limits: Factual QA, MuSiQue, QuALITY, GSM-Hard; corruption is injected into one answer-relevant fact. Adoption cuts are 5-10 points, not a fix. Judge-model labelling of reasoning traces.
agent_relevance: Gaps 7 and 9. Our agent's own tool outputs behave like any tool: adoption is high, and a verify-by-extra-tool-call instruction is the best accuracy/adoption balance. The authors' LLM-judge rule ('explicit statement that a return is wrong, suspicious, implausible or conflicts with another belief') is a workable detector of noticed-but-passed-through conflicts (gap 9).

source: Tian, Shi, Zhou, Zhao (2026) Beyond Function Calling: Benchmarking Tool-Using Agents under Tool-Environment Unreliability (ToolBench-X, arXiv 2606.25819)
finding: When tools misbehave but a recovery path exists, failure comes mainly from not diagnosing the hazard. A targeted recovery hint recovers most of the loss; extra test-time thinking helps less.
numbers: Five hazard types (spec drift, invocation error, execution failure, output drift, cross-source conflict). Gap between exception-injected baseline and clean oracle 35-50 points; hints lift accuracy by 25.5-35.5 points, recovering about 60-80% of the loss across 5 models. After the first failed call, retrying the same tool is 44-76% of next actions. Of failed trajectories, 48.6% were ineffective continuation and 26.7% early abandonment. Most models under 60% success.
limits: Deterministic toy tools, hints written by the authors and may leak structure; 200-task subset for recovery tests; test-time scaling was failure-triggered.
agent_relevance: Gap 2: the bottleneck is noticing and naming the anomaly, not effort. Retrying the same call 44-76% of the time is the agent version of local patching. An O-reframe trigger should fire on a repeated failed action and switch the question to 'what could be wrong with the environment or source'.

source: Muennighoff et al. (2025) s1: Simple test-time scaling (arXiv 2501.19393)
finding: Suppressing the end-of-thinking token and appending 'Wait' made a reasoning model re-check and often correct itself, with no external signal. 'Wait' beat other continuation strings.
numbers: s1-32B on AIME24: 50.0 without extrapolation, up to 57.6 in budget-forcing settings with 'Wait' (2x/4x/6x suppressions; exact cell per setting not resolved from the extracted table). 2x with no string and 2x 'Alternatively' stayed at 50.0.
quote: We find that 'Wait' generally gives the best performance.
limits: Math (AIME24, MATH500, GPQA), one SFT model of 1,000 samples; spends more tokens, so it is not an equal-token comparison; gain is on tasks where the model has the ability.
agent_relevance: Gap 3: second primary source that a neutral 'Wait' continuation helps reasoning models without telling them they are wrong. Together with Tsui (K09) it contrasts with Huang's null, which used prompts that ask the model to review its answer in a fresh turn. Still untested on staged-evidence tasks.

source: Petrova and Vejsiu (2026) Spectral Origins of the Self-Correction Blind Spot in Autoregressive Generation (arXiv 2607.09803)
finding: A formal model says the blind spot appears when the error-propagation operator has spectral radius at least one, and that a correction marker must exceed a threshold set by that radius. Fitted to four backbones.
numbers: Reports spectral predictions within 3.2% RMSE of measured blind-spot rates and 'recovers' the 89.3% reduction from Tsui; four backbones plus a visual autoregressive probe.
limits: Only the abstract and introduction were read. A theory paper by a small group, validated on their own backbones. It re-states Tsui's 64.5% and 89.3% as given, so it is not an independent replication.
agent_relevance: Do not count it as a second source for 'Wait' (K09). It only offers a mechanism story. Treat Tsui plus s1 as the evidence and this as a hypothesis.

source: Gulati et al. (2026) Ask Early, Ask Late, Ask Right: When Does Clarification Timing Matter for Long-Horizon Agents? (arXiv 2605.07937)
finding: A forced clarification is only valuable early for goal information and later for input information; late clarification is worse than never asking. Real models ask at the wrong times.
numbers: 84 task variants, 3 benchmarks, 4 models, 6,000+ runs (6,348, API cost about $4,200). Goal clarification loses nearly all value after 10% of the run (pass@3 0.78 to baseline); input clarification keeps value to about 50%. 300 unscripted sessions: GPT-5.2 asks in 52% of sessions (mean timing 43%), Claude Sonnet 4.5 asks selectively (23%, timing 50%), Gemini 3 Flash never asks.
limits: Ground-truth clarifications are injected, so it measures timing, not the quality of the question. Underspecification from the LHAW benchmark.
agent_relevance: Gap 5: a clarify operator has a window. Add a time component: ask about goals in the first tenth of a run. Asking late costs more than not asking.

source: Lord, Ross, Lepper (1979) Biased assimilation and attitude polarization (JPSP 37:2098-2109), seen via search result summaries only
finding: Per search summaries: 48 undergraduates (proponents and opponents of capital punishment) rated the study that agreed with them as more convincing and the same-method study that disagreed as flawed, and reported being more extreme after both. Attitude change was self-reported.
numbers: N=48 from summaries only. Original not opened (publisher and PDF hosts blocked).
limits: Not opened. Several replications cited in the summaries, none read.
agent_relevance: Do not rely on the figures. Gap 6 stays open for Lord.

source: Chinn and Brewer (1998) An empirical test of a taxonomy of responses to anomalous data in science (JRST 35:623-654), seen via search result summaries only
finding: Per search summaries: results generally supported the taxonomy but showed that one more response type (uncertainty about validity) was needed, giving eight. A secondary review says most undergraduate responses on a paper-and-pencil instrument were rejection (questioning validity, naming method problems).
numbers: No frequencies recovered. Wiley and Rutgers pages returned 403 or no text.
limits: Not opened. This is the gap-6 source that could not be reached.
agent_relevance: Use the eight-way list (adds 'uncertainty about validity') when coding agent responses. Do not quote frequencies from memory.

source: Search summaries for 'When Agents Trust the Wrong Tool Output' (NeurIPS 2026 listing) and Dunbar (1993) Concept discovery in a scientific domain
finding: Per a search summary, one prompt cut unsafe accepts of wrong tool outputs but raised deferral on reliable outputs from 1 in 50 to 33/50 and 30/50 in two settings. For Dunbar 1993 only secondary descriptions were found: one group of students kept seeking evidence for the original (wrong) hypothesis.
numbers: Summary only; no percentages for Dunbar 1993.
limits: Not opened. Treat both as pointers.
agent_relevance: The first item supports the Yang finding that the cost of a stricter prompt lands on valid tool outputs, so measure both. The Dunbar item leaves gap 6 open.
